KC_01.name: Arithmetic Mean
KC_01.description: Understanding the arithmetic mean as the center of a dataset.

KC_02.name: Standard Deviation
KC_02.description: Understanding standard deviation as a measure of variability around the mean.

KC_03.name: Standardized Distance
KC_03.description: Understanding differences between values or group means in units of standard deviations.

KC_04.name: Normal Distributions and Percentiles
KC_04.description: Understanding the relationship between standard deviations and percentile ranks under a normal-distribution assumption.

KC_05.name: Bloom's Experimental Conditions
KC_05.description: Understanding the conventional instruction, mastery learning, and tutoring conditions compared in Bloom's research.

KC_06.name: Mastery Learning
KC_06.description: Understanding formative assessment, feedback, corrective instruction, and reassessment.

KC_07.name: Experimental Evidence and Generalization
KC_07.description: Understanding the design, scope, and limits of Bloom's reported experiments.

KC_08.name: Bloom's Reported Results
KC_08.description: Understanding the approximately one-sigma mastery-learning result and two-sigma tutoring result.

KC_09.name: The 2 Sigma Problem
KC_09.description: Understanding Bloom's challenge of reproducing tutoring-level achievement through practical, scalable instruction.

KC_10.name: Application and Interpretation
KC_10.description: Understanding how Bloom's findings motivate adaptive learning without guaranteeing identical results across interventions.

stage-01-core.questionText:
Four students score 60, 70, 80, and 90 on a test.

What is the class mean?
stage-01-core.answerExplanation:
(60+70+80+90) / 4=75 

The mean gives a reference point for the center of these scores.

stage-01-transfer.questionText:
A class has an average test score of 72.

Every student's score is then increased by exactly 5 points.

What is the new mean?

choices.text: Cannot tell

stage-01-transfer.answerExplanation: Adding 5 to every observation increases the mean by 5.

stage-02-core.questionText:
Two classes both have a mean score of 80.

Class A's scores are mostly between 78 and 82.

Class B's scores are mostly between 60 and 100.

Which class has the larger standard deviation?

choices.text: Class A
Class B
They have the same standard deviation because their means are equal
Cannot be determined

stage-02-core.answerExplanation:
Standard deviation measures spread around the mean.

Class B's scores are much farther apart despite both classes having the same mean.

stage-02-transfer.questionText:
Every student in a class receives exactly 85 points.

What is the standard deviation?

choices.text: It depends on the number of students

stage-02-transfer.answerExplanation:
Every observation equals the mean.

There is no variability, so the standard deviation is zero.

stage-03-core.questionText:
A conventional class has a mean achievement score of 70 and a standard deviation of 6.

Another group's mean is 82.

How far above the conventional mean is the second group's mean?

choices.text: 1 standard deviation
2 standard deviations
6 standard deviations
12 standard deviations

stage-03-core.answerExplanation:
82 − 70 = 12; 12 ÷ 6 = 2.

The second mean is two conventional-group standard deviations above the conventional mean.

stage-03-transfer.questionText:
Imagine a graph where the conventional mean is at z=0.

The average for another instructional condition appears at z=+2.

What does that mean?

choices.text: Its mean is twice the conventional score
Its mean is two percentage points higher
Its mean is two conventional-group standard deviations higher
Every student improved by two standard deviations

stage-03-transfer.answerExplanation: A standardized distance of +2 indicates that the second group's mean is two reference-group standard deviations above the reference mean.

stage-04-core.questionText: In an approximately normal reference distribution, a score two standard deviations above the mean is closest to which percentile?

choices.text: 68th
84th
95th
98th

stage-04-core.answerExplanation:
For a normal distribution:

 z=2 

corresponds to approximately the 97.7th percentile.

This means approximately 97.7% of the reference distribution lies below that value.

stage-04-transfer.questionText:
A student is at approximately the 97.7th percentile of a normal reference population.

Which standardized score is closest?
stage-04-transfer.answerExplanation: Approximately 97.7% of a normal distribution lies below a value two standard deviations above its mean.

stage-05-core.questionText: Which set best matches the three instructional conditions described in Bloom's 1984 paper?

choices.text: Lecture, homework, final exam
Conventional classroom, mastery-learning classroom, tutoring
Public school, private school, homeschool
Human tutoring, computer tutoring, no instruction

stage-05-core.answerExplanation:
Bloom reported three instructional conditions:

Conventional classroom instruction.
Mastery-learning classroom instruction.
Tutoring.

The purpose was to compare student achievement under different instructional approaches.

stage-05-transfer.questionText:
A researcher creates three groups:

Normal classroom instruction.
Similar classroom instruction plus mastery procedures.
Individualized tutoring.

Which historical comparison is this attempting to reproduce?

choices.text: Bloom's comparison of conventional instruction, mastery learning, and tutoring
A comparison of students from three different schools
A comparison of three examinations
A comparison of three statistical distributions

stage-05-transfer.answerExplanation: Although the descriptions differ, the three instructional conditions have the same structure as Bloom's comparison.

stage-06-core.questionText: What was the central additional process used in Bloom's mastery-learning condition?

choices.text: Students simply spent twice as long studying
Formative testing → feedback → corrective instruction → a parallel formative test
Students selected whichever topics interested them
Students were placed in much smaller classes

stage-06-core.answerExplanation: Mastery learning uses formative assessment to identify gaps, feedback and corrective instruction to address them, and reassessment to check whether the learner has achieved mastery.

stage-06-transfer.questionText:
A student takes a short quiz and discovers that she cannot use conditional probability.

She receives targeted practice, then takes a different quiz on conditional probability before advancing.

Which aspect makes this mastery learning rather than ordinary grading?

choices.text: The student receives a numerical score.
Assessment identifies a gap, triggers corrective instruction, and is followed by reassessment before progression.
The student completes all questions without feedback.
The teacher gives every student the same additional lecture.

stage-06-transfer.answerExplanation: The assessment controls what happens next in the learning process rather than merely recording the student's performance.

stage-07-core.questionText: Which statement most accurately describes the studies Bloom summarized?

choices.text: Millions of students were followed across all school subjects for several years.
Students self-selected whether they wanted tutoring.
Four samples across grades 4, 5, and 8 studied Probability or Cartography; students were randomly assigned, and each sub-study lasted 11 instructional periods over three weeks.
The studies exclusively examined university mathematics students.

stage-07-core.answerExplanation: Four samples in grades 4, 5, and 8 studied Probability or Cartography. Students were randomly assigned; each sub-study lasted 11 instructional periods over three weeks. These were specific populations, subjects, and durations, not every educational setting.

stage-07-transfer.questionText: Which conclusion goes furthest beyond what those experiments alone establish?

choices.text: Large achievement differences appeared in those particular instructional comparisons.
Bloom thought tutoring provided an important benchmark.
Every subject, age group, tutor, and future tutoring system should produce a 2σ effect.
Mastery learning was also compared with conventional instruction.

stage-07-transfer.answerExplanation: Evidence from particular experiments cannot establish that an identical effect will occur under every possible instructional condition.

stage-08-core.questionText: Which summary matches the result Bloom reported?

choices.text: Mastery learning ≈ +2σ; tutoring ≈ +1σ
Mastery learning ≈ +1σ; tutoring ≈ +2σ
Both treatments ≈ +2σ
Neither differed substantially from conventional instruction

stage-08-core.answerExplanation:
Using the conventional group’s standard deviation (σ) as the reference:

Mean(mastery) ≈ Mean(conventional) + 1σ
Mean(tutoring) ≈ Mean(conventional) + 2σ

These are differences between group means, expressed in conventional-group standard deviation units.

stage-08-transfer.questionText:
Suppose the conventional achievement distribution is standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.

Which approximate pair represents Bloom's reported group means?

choices.text: Mastery = 0, Tutoring = 1
Mastery = 1, Tutoring = 2
Mastery = 2, Tutoring = 4
Mastery = −1, Tutoring = −2

stage-08-transfer.answerExplanation:
Relative to the conventional mean:

Mastery learning: approximately +1σ.
Tutoring: approximately +2σ.

choices.text: Determine why standard deviation is represented by sigma.
Find a cheaper statistical test for educational experiments.
Find practical group-instruction methods capable of approaching the achievement attained under effective tutoring.
Prove that every student needs a private tutor.

stage-09-core.answerExplanation: Bloom identified the challenge of achieving tutoring-like educational outcomes through practical instructional methods that could be provided to large numbers of learners.

stage-09-transfer.questionText: Which research project is most directly attempting to address Bloom's problem?

choices.text: Finding a new symbol for standard deviation.
Building an affordable instructional system that adapts feedback and remediation to individual learners, then testing whether it approaches tutoring-level outcomes.
Hiring one private human tutor for every learner regardless of cost.
Replacing all assessments with lectures.

stage-09-transfer.answerExplanation:
The proposed system attempts to provide the benefits of individualized instruction without requiring an individual human tutor for every student.

Its effectiveness would still need to be established experimentally.

stage-10-core.questionText:
A company builds an adaptive AI tutor that gives every learner personalized questions and remediation.

Which statement is scientifically justified from Bloom's work alone?

choices.text: Because it is personalized, it will automatically improve achievement by 2σ.
Bloom proves that every AI tutor performs as well as a strong human tutor.
The system addresses the kind of scalable individualized-instruction problem Bloom highlighted, but its actual learning effect must be measured experimentally.
If it uses mastery learning, a +1σ gain is guaranteed.

stage-10-core.answerExplanation:
Bloom's findings provide a motivating benchmark and research problem.

They do not establish the performance of a future instructional system.

An adaptive system needs independent experimental evidence to establish its actual effectiveness.

stage-10-transfer.questionText:
A new adaptive platform runs a randomized controlled trial and finds an achievement effect of +0.35 standard deviations compared with ordinary instruction.

Which interpretation is strongest?

choices.text: It failed because Bloom proved successful tutoring must achieve +2 standard deviations.
It solved Bloom's problem because every adaptive system automatically counts as a solution.
It produced a measured positive effect; comparison with Bloom's 2σ benchmark requires attention to differences in intervention, population, outcome, and experimental design.
+0.35 standard deviations means students learned 35% more material.

stage-10-transfer.answerExplanation: Standardized achievement effects can be compared descriptively, but their interpretation depends on the instructional approach, learner population, comparison condition, assessment, and experimental design.

stage-01-explanation.title: Arithmetic Mean — explained
stage-01-explanation.content:
The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of numbers.

Add every value together and divide by the number of values.

If every observation changes by the same amount, the mean changes by that amount too.

Bloom's research compares the average achievement of different groups, so understanding the mean is necessary before interpreting his findings.

stage-02-explanation.title: Standard Deviation — explained
stage-02-explanation.content:
The mean describes where the center of a dataset is.

Standard deviation describes how spread out the observations are around that center.

Two groups can have identical means but different standard deviations.

If every observation has the same value, the standard deviation is zero.

stage-03-explanation.title: Standardized Distance — explained
stage-03-explanation.content:
Sigma, written σ, represents standard deviation.

A difference of 2σ means a separation equal to twice the reference group's standard deviation.

It does not mean the score doubled.

For example, if the conventional mean is 70 and its standard deviation is 6, then a mean two standard deviations higher is:

 70+2(6)=82

stage-04-explanation.title: Normal Distributions and Percentiles — explained
stage-04-explanation.content:
In a normal distribution, approximately 95.4% of observations lie within two standard deviations of the mean.

That leaves approximately 2.3% of observations above +2σ.

A value at +2σ is therefore around the 97.7th percentile.

Bloom described the average tutored student as performing above approximately 98% of conventional students.

This does not mean 98% of tutored students were above the conventional mean.

stage-05-explanation.title: Bloom's Experimental Conditions — explained
stage-05-explanation.content:
Bloom compared three approaches to instruction:

Conventional instruction involved ordinary group teaching.

Mastery learning added formative testing and corrective procedures to group instruction.

Tutoring provided highly individualized instruction, while also using formative assessment and feedback.

Understanding these conditions is necessary before comparing their reported outcomes.

stage-06-explanation.title: Mastery Learning — explained
stage-06-explanation.content:
In ordinary grading, a test may simply measure how well a student performed before the class continues.

In mastery learning, assessments are used to identify missing knowledge.

Students receive targeted corrective instruction and are reassessed before progressing.

The central cycle is:

 Assessment → Feedback → Correction → Reassessment

stage-07-explanation.title: Experimental Evidence and Generalization — explained
stage-07-explanation.content:
Bloom summarized four samples across grades 4, 5, and 8 studying Probability or Cartography, with random assignment and 11 instructional periods over three weeks per sub-study.

An experiment can establish findings for the specific population, intervention, and outcome measures that were studied.

It does not automatically establish that the same results will occur across all other settings.

Bloom's studies provide evidence about particular instructional comparisons.

Their reported effect sizes should not be interpreted as a universal guarantee for all tutoring systems.

stage-08-explanation.title: Bloom's Reported Results — explained
stage-08-explanation.content:
Bloom reported two important comparisons.

The mastery-learning group had an average achievement level approximately one conventional-group standard deviation above the conventional mean.

The tutoring group had an average achievement level approximately two conventional-group standard deviations above the conventional mean.

Remember:

 Conventional = 0σ
Mastery = +1σ
Tutoring = +2σ 

The values describe standardized differences between group averages.

stage-09-explanation.title: The 2 Sigma Problem — explained
stage-09-explanation.content:
Bloom's finding and Bloom's problem are different things.

Finding: The tutoring group performed approximately two conventional-group standard deviations above the conventional mean.

Problem: How can educators reproduce similarly strong learning outcomes using instructional methods that are affordable and practical for large numbers of students?

The problem concerns scalable instructional design.

stage-10-explanation.title: Application and Interpretation — explained
stage-10-explanation.content:
Bloom's result describes the achievement differences observed in particular instructional experiments.

It does not guarantee a two-standard-deviation improvement for every future tutoring or adaptive-learning system.

An adaptive platform may address Bloom's scalability challenge by providing individualized instruction to many learners.

However, its actual learning effect must be measured independently.
